title: What is a Pandas UDF (vectorized UDF) — it transfers data in batches via Apache Arrow instead of row-by-row, and your function operates on a `pd.Series`, giving 10-100x speedup over plain UDFs — and how do you enable Arrow (`spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled=true`)?

s1_definition.profdef: A Pandas UDF, also called a vectorized UDF, is a PySpark user-defined function that operates on batches of data instead of one row at a time. Spark uses Apache Arrow to transfer a column of values as a pandas Series to the Python worker, your function processes the whole Series with vectorized pandas or NumPy operations, and the result Series is shipped back via Arrow. This amortizes the JVM-to-Python boundary cost across many rows, giving a 10 to 100 times speedup over a plain row-at-a-time Python UDF. Arrow is enabled by setting `spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled` to true.
s1_definition.analogy: A plain UDF mails the National Bank's transactions to a Python analyst one letter at a time, paying postage on each. A Pandas UDF ships a whole box of transactions at once; the analyst processes the entire box with a single sweep and ships the box back. Same work, almost no postage per item, so it finishes far faster.
s1_definition.oneliner: A Pandas UDF processes a whole column at once via Arrow batches as a pandas Series, turning per-row overhead into per-batch overhead.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Pandas UDF, also called a vectorized UDF, is a PySpark user-defined function that operates on batches of data instead of one row at a time. Spark uses Apache Arrow to transfer a column of values as a pandas Series to the Python worker, your function processes the whole Series with vectorized pandas or NumPy operations, and the result Series is shipped back via Arrow. This amortizes the JVM-to-Python boundary cost across many rows, giving a 10 to 100 times speedup over a plain row-at-a-time Python UDF. Arrow is enabled by setting `spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled` to true.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A plain UDF mails the National Bank's transactions to a Python analyst one letter at a time, paying postage on each. A Pandas UDF ships a whole box of transactions at once; the analyst processes the entire box with a single sweep and ships the box back. Same work, almost no postage per item, so it finishes far faster.

**One line to remember:** A Pandas UDF processes a whole column at once via Arrow batches as a pandas Series, turning per-row overhead into per-batch overhead.

sections.s2_technical:
The slowness of a plain UDF comes from serializing and crossing the JVM-to-Python boundary for every row. A Pandas UDF fixes the mechanism: Apache Arrow is a columnar in-memory format that both the JVM and Python understand without converting object by object. Spark groups rows into batches, encodes each batch in Arrow, hands it to Python as a pandas Series, and your function runs vectorized operations over the entire Series at C speed.

You declare one with the `pandas_udf` decorator and a return type: `@pandas_udf(DoubleType())` followed by `def fee(amount: pd.Series) -> pd.Series: return amount * 0.001`. There are several flavors. A Series-to-Series UDF maps one or more input columns to one output column. A Series-to-scalar UDF is used as an aggregate, for example `@pandas_udf(DoubleType())` with `def mean_amt(a: pd.Series) -> float: return a.mean()` used in `groupBy(...).agg(mean_amt("amount"))`. An iterator-of-Series UDF lets you initialize an expensive resource once per partition, for example loading a model, then process many batches.

To enable the Arrow transfer you set `spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled` to true, either in `spark-defaults.conf` or at runtime with `spark.conf.set("spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled", "true")`. You can also tune the batch size with `spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch`. If Arrow is disabled or an unsupported type appears, Spark falls back to slower non-Arrow conversion, so you confirm it is on.

A senior nuance: Pandas UDFs still cannot be optimized through by Catalyst the way built-ins can, so a built-in expression is still faster when one exists. Use Pandas UDFs when you need genuine Python or a library like NumPy, scikit-learn, or custom math that has no SQL equivalent, and prefer the iterator form when there is expensive per-partition setup.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank must apply a custom risk-scoring formula to millions of transactions that uses a NumPy function with no Spark built-in equivalent. A plain Python UDF was too slow. This is exactly where a Series-to-Series Pandas UDF helps, processing whole batches via Arrow.

Problem 2 — The risk team also needs a per-account average exposure, computed with a custom aggregate. This is exactly the Series-to-scalar Pandas UDF used inside groupBy.

Problem 3 — A later model-scoring step loads a heavy scoring object that is expensive to build. This is exactly the iterator-of-Series form, which initializes once per partition.

What the code will do: a PySpark demo (`PandasUdfDemo`) that enables Arrow, computes a vectorized risk score with a Series-to-Series Pandas UDF, computes per-account average amount with a Series-to-scalar Pandas UDF, and demonstrates an iterator UDF — for Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001).

sections.s4d_java:
```python
# File: src/pandas_udf_demo.py
# Demonstrates vectorized Pandas UDFs for risk scoring at the National Bank of India.
import logging
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
from scoring.risk_udfs import risk_score_udf, avg_amount_udf, scaled_score_iter

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("PandasUdfDemo")

def spark_session() -> SparkSession:
    spark = (SparkSession.builder.appName("PandasUdfDemo")
             .config("spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled", "true")
             .getOrCreate())
    log.info("Arrow enabled: %s",
             spark.conf.get("spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled"))
    return spark

def main() -> None:
    spark = spark_session()
    txns = spark.createDataFrame(
        [("TXN-1", "SAV2001", 50000.0), ("TXN-2", "CUR3001", 25000.0),
         ("TXN-3", "SAV2001", 12000.0), ("TXN-4", "CUR3001", 90000.0)],
        ["txn_id", "account_id", "amount"])

    # Series -> Series: vectorized risk score over the whole amount column
    scored = txns.withColumn("risk_score", risk_score_udf("amount"))
    log.info("Vectorized risk scores:")
    scored.show()

    # Series -> scalar: custom aggregate per account
    avg = txns.groupBy("account_id").agg(avg_amount_udf("amount").alias("avg_amt"))
    log.info("Per-account average amount (Pandas UDF aggregate):")
    avg.show()

    # Iterator-of-Series: expensive setup once per partition
    iter_scored = txns.withColumn("scaled", scaled_score_iter("amount"))
    log.info("Iterator-UDF scaled scores:")
    iter_scored.show()
    spark.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```python
# File: src/scoring/risk_udfs.py
from typing import Iterator
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from pyspark.sql.functions import pandas_udf
from pyspark.sql.types import DoubleType

# Series -> Series: operates on an entire pandas Series per Arrow batch
@pandas_udf(DoubleType())
def risk_score_udf(amount: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    # vectorized NumPy: no Spark built-in equivalent for this custom formula
    return pd.Series(np.log1p(amount.to_numpy()) * 1.5)

# Series -> scalar: used as a custom aggregate inside groupBy().agg()
@pandas_udf(DoubleType())
def avg_amount_udf(amount: pd.Series) -> float:
    return float(amount.mean())

# Iterator-of-Series: build an expensive resource ONCE, reuse across batches
@pandas_udf(DoubleType())
def scaled_score_iter(it: Iterator[pd.Series]) -> Iterator[pd.Series]:
    scaler = 0.0001          # pretend this is an expensive-to-load model/config
    for batch in it:
        yield batch * scaler
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four transactions with amounts for Rajesh and Priya.

Step 1: The SparkSession is built with Arrow enabled, and the demo logs the setting to confirm the fast path is active.

Step 2: For the Series-to-Series risk score, Spark groups the amount column into Arrow batches and hands each to Python as a pandas Series. The function applies `np.log1p(amount) * 1.5` vectorized over the whole Series and returns it. The result becomes the `risk_score` column.

Step 3: For the Series-to-scalar aggregate, Spark groups rows by `account_id`, hands each group's amounts to the function as a Series, and the function returns the mean. SAV2001 averages its two amounts, CUR3001 averages its two.

Step 4: For the iterator UDF, Spark hands the Python worker an iterator of Series per partition; the function builds the scaler once, then multiplies each batch, which is how you avoid repeating expensive setup.

Step 5: All results are regular DataFrame columns, so downstream operations continue on the JVM.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Pandas UDF, or vectorized UDF, is a PySpark function that works on batches of data rather than one row at a time. The mechanism is Apache Arrow, a columnar in-memory format both the JVM and Python understand without converting value by value. Spark groups rows into batches, encodes each batch in Arrow, hands it to the Python worker as a pandas Series, my function runs vectorized pandas or NumPy operations over the whole Series, and the result comes back the same way. Because the expensive JVM-to-Python boundary crossing now happens once per batch instead of once per row, a Pandas UDF is typically ten to a hundred times faster than a plain row-at-a-time Python UDF.

There are a few flavors I use depending on the shape of the work. A Series-to-Series UDF maps input columns to an output column and is my default for custom row-wise math. A Series-to-scalar UDF acts as a custom aggregate inside groupBy and agg, for example a mean or a custom exposure metric per account. And an iterator-of-Series UDF lets me build an expensive resource like a loaded model once per partition and then process many batches with it, which avoids repeating costly setup. I enable the fast path by setting spark dot sql dot execution dot arrow dot pyspark dot enabled to true, and I can tune the batch size with maxRecordsPerBatch.

At the National Bank of India I reached for Pandas UDFs whenever the logic needed real Python with no Spark built-in equivalent. A custom risk-scoring formula that used a NumPy function ran far too slowly as a plain UDF, so I rewrote it as a Series-to-Series Pandas UDF and it processed millions of transactions in a fraction of the time. I used the Series-to-scalar form for a custom per-account average and the iterator form when a later step loaded a heavy scoring object. The important caveat I always add is that a Pandas UDF still cannot be optimized through by Catalyst, so if a pure built-in expression exists I use that first, and I only reach for a Pandas UDF when I genuinely need Python.
